paras: The Spring Valley race riot of 1895 was an attack on Sunday, August 4, 1895, by a mob of several hundred miners on "The Location," a Black miners' settlement near the No. 3 shaft at Spring Valley, Illinois, that drove its residents from their homes. Wire reports named fourteen Black men, women and children who were shot, clubbed or trampled, and the next day a mass meeting of miners ordered the remaining Black residents out of town. Local and outside accounts disputed how many were hurt or killed, and the expelled miners returned to work under guard on August 9.

An Associated Press dispatch reported "much feeling" against the coal company's manager, Dalzell, for allegedly bringing in Black miners, while the Princeton wire said the Italian miners had long wished to drive them out. Around midnight before the attack a man was robbed and shot near the settlement; the Princeton wire called him an Italian waylaid by four Black men, while the AP named him as Barney Role, a white man held up by five "colored men."

According to the AP, miners marched behind a brass band to Dalzell's house to demand the discharge of every Black man, and when he refused, a mob of 500, by the Princeton wire's count over 300 Italians, marched on the settlement. Men were dragged from their homes, clubbed, trampled and shot at, two women were shot, and houses were smashed and ransacked. Among the injured were Granville Lewis, shot and clubbed with rifles, and fourteen-year-old Maria Bird, shot in the breast.

By noon every Black resident had fled, and armed men spent the afternoon "hunting for negroes to shoot at," while those left behind were told to leave or be "shot down in their tracks." Sheriff Clark arrived with deputies after it was over, and no arrests were attempted.

On August 5 armed Italians kept miners from work, and over 2,000 miners resolved to give the remaining Black residents until 5 p.m. the next day to leave and demanded that the company discharge all Black workers. The company refused, a crowd tried to mob a newspaper correspondent, and the sheriff and state's attorney said they expected no successful prosecution.

In Chicago two refugees, Mary Stanton and Lizzie Dixdee, told a mass meeting the reports were not exaggerated; Stanton's two sons had disappeared, and Dixdee believed her husband dead. Representative John C. Buckner of Chicago took the case to Governor Altgeld, who promised protection but sent no troops.

On August 7 a miners' meeting voted to recognize the Fourteenth Amendment and let the Black miners return, though Italian crowds blocked the mines again the next day. On August 9 the Black miners came back with Buckner at their head and went down the No. 3 mine under a guard of about fifty deputies. Later briefs said eleven of the mob were held to the grand jury, twenty-three held for trial, or over thirty arrested; no report of a trial was found. A labor bureau investigation blamed the Black residents and recommended their removal.

The Princeton wire ran under headlines such as "Italians Attack Negroes" in the New-York Tribune and "Stiletto vs. Razor" in the Daily Kennebec Journal. The AP version appeared in a California Herald under "Because of Their Outrages" and in the Rock Island Argus with a subhead on the residents' "Criminal Record," even as it said the rioters "acted as so many fiends." Spring Valley dispatches soon denounced the Chicago papers, and a Chicago Post special said the race war existed only in a correspondent's imagination.

Editorials turned the episode to other quarrels: the Sacramento Record-Union's "Anarchy in Illinois" blamed unnaturalized Italians and Altgeld, the DeLamar Nugget blamed "dago" labor, and the Alexandria Gazette used the labor bureau report against abolition. The Springfield Republican mocked the bureau's finding that Black miners were the aggressors. All the coverage found is from white papers, with Black voices appearing only as quoted in them.

The Princeton wire named fourteen seriously injured, the AP revised its count to two fatally and twelve severely injured, and Buckner cited private word of thirty-four bodies. Against these, the mayor told the governor that no lives were lost and three were slightly injured, and the local AP correspondent said he found one man with a flesh wound. C. W. Bush, who visited Seatonville for Chicago's Black organizations, found the reports "substantially correct" and counted six badly and two slightly injured; no report confirming a Black death was found.

reader.title: Spring Valley race riot of 1895
bases: A mob of several hundred miners attacked the Black company settlement known as the Location, beating and shooting residents and driving all of them out, followed by a mass-meeting order expelling those who remained (A3, A4, A6).

The Princeton wire and the separate AP Spring Valley dispatch agree that a mob attacked the settlement and drove the Black residents out, and even the local accounts that minimized injuries admit the expulsion (A3, A4, A12); the number hurt or killed is contested (A16, A19).

accounts.label: Princeton wire
accounts.gist: Italian miners, long wishing to drive Black workers out, used the shooting of an Italian as an excuse; a mob of 300 led by a band attacked the village, shot fourteen named people and drove out the rest.

accounts.label: AP Spring Valley dispatch
accounts.gist: 500 miners marched on Dalzell after Barney Role was robbed and shot by five colored men, then attacked the Location; first two shot not seriously, later two fatally and twelve severely; blames 'outrages' charged to Black residents.

accounts.label: Spring Valley townspeople and mayor
accounts.gist: No attempt was made to kill, only to scare the residents away; one or three slightly hurt; reports of bodies were 'made of whole cloth.'

accounts.label: Refugee women in Chicago
accounts.gist: Mary Stanton and Lizzie Dixdee said the reports were not exaggerated, women and children were beaten, and their husband and sons were missing and believed dead.

accounts.label: Representative Buckner
accounts.gist: From private information, thirty-four bodies had been found and about fourteen badly wounded.

accounts.label: C. W. Bush, Chicago investigator
accounts.gist: After visiting Seatonville he found the reports of wounding and clubbing substantially correct; six badly injured, two slightly.

accounts.label: Chicago Post special
accounts.gist: Two Black residents slightly injured and one Italian shot; the race war was imagined by the Princeton correspondent.

accounts.label: Illinois labor bureau report
accounts.gist: The Black residents were to blame and should be removed; 'all citizens sided with the Italians.'

framing.detail: 'ITALIANS ATTACK NEGROES' and 'A FIERCE OUTBURST OF RACE HATRED'; the Italians fell on the village 'like a lot of Apache Indians'.
AP headline 'BECAUSE OF THEIR OUTRAGES' and 'Imported Colored Men', with a 'Criminal Record' subhead in Rock Island, yet the rioters 'acted as so many fiends'.
Local dispatches 'STILL DENOUNCE CHICAGO PAPERS', say whites endured 'the outrages of the blacks' and call death reports invented.
Chicago Post special: the race war 'exists only in the imagination' of a correspondent.
Sacramento editorial 'ANARCHY IN ILLINOIS' condemns 'murderous aliens' and Altgeld, calling the victims American citizens.
DeLamar Nugget editorial blames mine owners and 'dago' labor, hostile to both groups.
Alexandria Gazette quotes the labor bureau's blame of the Black residents to jab at abolition.
Springfield Republican mocks the labor bureau's finding that the negro was the aggressor.

'The Location', a settlement of about 100 company houses near the No. 3 shaft, about two miles west of Spring Valley

Marty), Norman Bird, Mrs. Bird, Maria Bird (14), William Lee, Jube Sterritt, Oscar Prim, Silas Burken (or Burner), Jude Stuart, Jim Kelley, Will Beck, Frank Turner, Frank Burns (or Burner); the whole settlement driven out

Italian miners of Spring Valley per the Princeton wire and the AP's later paragraphs; 'white miners' in the AP's first paragraphs
